toLevel3.stem: Why does the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shift to the right at higher temperatures?
toLevel3.answer: More particles have higher kinetic energies on average
distractors: The total number of particles increases at higher temperature
The activation energy of the reaction decreases with heat
Particles lose energy and slow down at higher temperatures

toLevel3.stem: Why does the area under the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve stay the same at different temperatures?
toLevel3.answer: The total number of particles does not change
distractors: The activation energy remains constant at all temperatures
Energy is conserved so the curve cannot change area
The particles gain and lose energy in equal amounts

toLevel3.stem: Why does the high-temperature curve become shorter when it broadens?
toLevel3.answer: The area must stay constant, so a wider spread requires a lower peak
distractors: Particles are destroyed at higher temperatures reducing the peak
The activation energy increases at higher temperatures compressing the peak
Fewer particles exist at higher temperatures so the peak decreases

toLevel3.stem: What does the rightward shift of the high-temperature curve tell us about particle energy?
toLevel3.answer: A greater proportion of particles have higher kinetic energy
distractors: A greater proportion of particles have lost kinetic energy
All particles now have exactly the same kinetic energy
The average kinetic energy has decreased overall

toLevel3.stem: Why is the low-temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann curve narrower than the high-temperature curve?
toLevel3.answer: Particles have a smaller range of kinetic energies at lower temperatures
distractors: There are fewer particles present at lower temperatures overall
Particles at lower temperatures cannot collide with each other
The activation energy is lower at reduced temperatures

toLevel3.stem: What does the broader tail on the right side of a high-temperature curve indicate?
toLevel3.answer: More particles have very high kinetic energies
distractors: Fewer particles exist in the system overall
The activation energy has been lowered by the heat
Particles are moving more slowly on average

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at 25°C and needs to draw a second curve at 50°C on the same axes. Which description is correct?
toLevel4.answer: The 50°C curve should be shorter, broader, and shifted right
distractors: The 50°C curve should be taller, narrower, and shifted left
The 50°C curve should be identical to the 25°C curve
The 50°C curve should be taller, broader, and shifted right

toLevel4.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at 4°C is drawn with a peak at a certain kinetic energy. When the temperature rises to 37°C, how does the peak change?
toLevel4.answer: It moves to a higher kinetic energy and becomes lower in height
distractors: It moves to a lower kinetic energy and becomes taller
It stays at the same kinetic energy but doubles in height
It moves to a higher kinetic energy and becomes taller

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to draw two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves on the same diagram. They draw the high-temperature curve with a greater area than the low-temperature curve. What error have they made?
toLevel4.answer: The area under both curves should be equal
distractors: The high-temperature curve should have a smaller area
The curves should not be drawn on the same diagram
The low-temperature curve should have no area at all

toLevel4.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, the activation energy is marked with a vertical line. At higher temperature, the area to the right of this line is larger. What does this indicate?
toLevel4.answer: More particles have enough energy to react
distractors: The activation energy has decreased
Fewer particles are present in the system
The reaction has become endothermic

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a low-temperature curve with a peak at 10 kJ and a high-temperature curve with a peak at 20 kJ. Both curves are the same height. What correction should the student make?
toLevel4.answer: The high-temperature curve should be shorter than the low-temperature curve
distractors: The low-temperature curve should be shorter than the high-temperature curve
Both curves should be taller than originally drawn
The peaks should be at the same kinetic energy value

toLevel4.stem: A reaction mixture is cooled from 60°C to 20°C. How would the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve change?
toLevel4.answer: The peak becomes taller, narrower, and shifts to the left
distractors: The peak becomes shorter, broader, and shifts to the right
The peak stays in the same position but becomes taller
The curve disappears because particles stop moving

toLevel4.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram shows curves at 300 K and 500 K. The activation energy line is drawn at 40 kJ. Which curve shows a greater proportion of particles exceeding 40 kJ?
distractors: The 300 K curve
Both curves show the same proportion
Neither curve shows particles above 40 kJ

toLevel5.stem: A student draws two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves at different temperatures. The high-temperature curve is broader but its peak is the same height as the low-temperature curve. What is wrong with this diagram?
toLevel5.answer: The broader curve should have a lower peak to keep the total area constant
distractors: The broader curve should have a higher peak to show more energy
Both curves should always have the same width regardless of temperature
The curves should not overlap at any point on the diagram

toLevel5.stem: Two Maxwell-Boltzmann curves are drawn at T₁ and T₂ where T₂ > T₁. The area to the right of the Ea line is much larger for T₂. What can be concluded about the reaction rate at T₂?
toLevel5.answer: The rate is significantly faster because many more particles exceed Ea
distractors: The rate is slower because the peak is lower at T₂
The rate is unchanged because the total area is the same
The rate is slower because the activation energy has increased

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that raising the temperature from 300 K to 310 K has a negligible effect on the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shape. However, the reaction rate doubles. How can this be explained?
toLevel5.answer: Even a small shift in the curve can greatly increase the area beyond Ea in the tail region
distractors: The activation energy decreases by half when temperature rises by 10 K
The total number of particles doubles with a 10 K temperature increase
The curve shape does not affect reaction rate in any meaningful way

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'At higher temperature, all particles have more energy, so the entire curve shifts to the right uniformly.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — the curve broadens and flattens, not just shifts uniformly to the right
distractors: Correct — every particle gains the same amount of kinetic energy
Correct — the curve maintains its shape and simply moves rightward
Incorrect — the curve shifts to the left at higher temperatures

toLevel5.stem: Why does a small increase in temperature sometimes cause a large increase in reaction rate, even though the curve shape changes only slightly?
toLevel5.answer: The Ea line sits in the tail region where small shifts produce large area changes
distractors: A small temperature change completely eliminates the activation energy
The total number of particles increases dramatically with small temperature rises
Small temperature changes cause the curve to become perfectly flat

toLevel5.stem: A peer argues that because the area under both curves is equal, the reaction rate must also be equal at both temperatures. Is this reasoning valid?
toLevel5.answer: No — equal area means equal particle numbers, not equal proportions exceeding Ea
distractors: Yes — equal area always means equal reaction rates at any temperature
No — equal area means the high-temperature curve has fewer particles
Yes — the area under the curve directly represents the reaction rate

toLevel5.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann curve at a very high temperature has a very low, broad peak. What does this tell us about the distribution of particle energies?
toLevel5.answer: Particles have a very wide range of energies with no dominant energy value
distractors: All particles have nearly identical high kinetic energies
Most particles have zero kinetic energy at this temperature
The particles have stopped moving due to the extreme temperature

toLevel5.stem: A student draws a high-temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann curve that does not start at the origin on the x-axis. Is this a valid representation?
toLevel5.answer: No — all Maxwell-Boltzmann curves must start at zero kinetic energy
distractors: Yes — high-temperature curves can start at any kinetic energy
Yes — the starting point depends on the activation energy
No — all curves must start at the activation energy value
